title: Turing Post (@TheTuringPost)
summary:
We’ve learned how to build skilled agents, but still don’t know how to run them as a team.
Huawei Noah’s Ark Lab proposed OneManCompany (OMC) – an organisational layer for multi-agent systems that treats agents like employees in a real company.
The main idea is to move from Skills → Talents
A Skill is a tool/function inside one agent. But a Talent is a full agent package: role, tools, skills, prompts, configs, and working principles.
So OMC can "hire" a specialist agent.
The system has 3 main pillars:
1. Talent + Container = Employee
Talent = who the agent is: developer, designer, researcher, etc.
Container = where it runs, like Claude Code, LangGraph, scripts, etc.
So different kinds of agents can work together in one organisation through shared interfaces.
2. Talent Market
If the current team lacks a capability, OMC can recruit a new "specialist" from a marketplace of verified agents. The agent team is fully configurable
3. E2R tree search: Explore–Execute–Review loop
- explores how to decompose the task
- assigns subtasks to agents
- executes them
- reviews outputs before they can unblock downstream work
- retries or re-decomposes when something fails
Tasks form a dynamic tree/DAG with review gates, so bad intermediate outputs don’t silently propagate. Plus, agents update their own working principles after tasks and feedback.
There is even an HR-style lifecycle: performance reviews → Performance Improvement Plan (PIP) → offboarding → replacement from the Talent Market.
OMC proved its efficiency, reaching 84.67% success on PRDBench, about 15 percentage points better than previous baselines. So this is a strategy worth taking a closer look at.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HHGbBMHbgAA6Knf.jpg

title: Turing Post (@TheTuringPost)
summary:
Models gain a lot from long reasoning but maybe they don’t need to write reasoning in words at all?
@IBM introduced Abstract Chain-of-Thought that replaces text reasoning with abstract tokens.
The model produces a short sequence with these special tokens which are:
- much shorter
- not human-readable
- and act like a hidden scratchpad.
The difficult part is that these tokens start as meaningless, so the model is trained in 2 phases:
1. Compression from CoT, when it takes normal reasoning and compresses it into abstract tokens
2. Self-distillation: Remove the text reasoning completely and the model trains to generate abstract tokens directly.
Then everything is refined with RL.
The results are about real efficiency:
Abstract-CoT needs up to 11.6× fewer reasoning tokens -> inference in much cheaper with similar performance to normal CoT
And another interesting thing - the abstract tokens start behaving like a real language, and the model learns its own internal reasoning language
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HHHG1s_aAAAkxNI.jpg

title: Turing Post (@TheTuringPost)
summary:
The "magic" of embedding lies in total generalization
Embeddings are the step where pieces of language stop being just tokens and turn into a form a model can actually work with.
-> Token IDs move from integers into geometry, where distance represents meaning and connection between words.
Concepts become vectors in a continuous space. Similar items are mapped to nearby points in this space, so:
- Similar words (like cat, kitten, tiger) → similar vectors
- Similar sentences → similar structure
This forms a sense of the full context.
In Transformers, embeddings become contextual: the vector for a token depends on the entire sequence and evolves across layers during processing.
That's why embeddings are a core interface between models and real-world data – they store meaning as searchable vectors for similarity search, transfer learning, retrieval and multimodal alignment. None of this would really be possible without embeddings.

title: Turing Post (@TheTuringPost)
summary:
.@NVIDIA explored how speculative decoding can speed up RL without changing the model’s behavior.
->The result is up to ~2.5× faster end-to-end RL at 235B scale
Speculative decoding is when a smaller "draft" model predicts several next tokens at once, and the main model verifies them. If the predictions are correct, the system accepts multiple tokens in one step.
This method has an important advantage for reinforcement learning - it is lossless: the final sampled sequence follows the same distribution as the original large model. This means the policy learns from its own true outputs.
The researchers showed that speculative decoding indeed can be integrated into full RL training pipelines where:
- policy weights constantly change
- rollout workers need synchronization
- logprobs and KL penalties must stay correct
They made this work reliably inside NeMo-RL + vLLM stack, and that resulted in ~1.8× faster rollout throughput at 8B scale as well.
The core finding here: speed optimization in RL comes primary from how tokens are generated. And speculative decoding speeds up this generation -> speeds up RL.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HHrPQ6haUAAkPtf.png

title: Turing Post (@TheTuringPost)
summary:
Distribution-Guided Policy Optimization (DGPO) – a new PO method that shifts focus to rewarding useful exploration
DGPO improves famous GRPO. It identifies which reasoning steps really mattered:
1. Like GRPO, DGPO samples several Chain-of-Thought reasoning paths for comparison.
2. A verifier/reward model scores the final answers, and DGPO computes a sequence-level advantage.
It selectively redistributes rewards instead of giving every token the same one.
3. DGPO replaces unstable KL divergence with bounded Hellinger distance that measures how much the model’s token predictions deviate from the reference model.
It compares the square roots of the probabilities that two models assign to the same tokens.
Deviation from the reference model becomes a signal of potential reasoning innovation.
4. Entropy gating filters hallucinations. High entropy → genuine exploration, low entropy → confident hallucination.
5. Tokens responsible for successful reasoning receive larger updates.
▪️ Why DGPO is a good new option:
• Exploration is rewarded and no critic model is needed
• Better token-level reasoning supervision
• More stable than KL-based RL
• Strong improvements on long reasoning tasks like math benchmarks: AIME 2025: 46.0%, AIME 2024 60.0%. It's better than methods like DAPO

Speculative decoding is when a smaller "draft" model predicts several next tokens at once, and the main model verifies them. If the predictions are correct, the system accepts multiple tokens in one step.
This method has an important advantage for reinforcement learning - it is lossless: the final sampled sequence follows the same distribution as the original large model. This means the policy learns from its own true outputs.
The researchers showed that speculative decoding indeed can be integrated into full RL training pipelines where:
- policy weights constantly change
- rollout workers need synchronization
- logprobs and KL penalties must stay correct
They made this work reliably inside NeMo-RL + vLLM stack, and that resulted in ~1.8× faster rollout throughput at 8B scale as well.
The core finding here: speed optimization in RL comes primary from how tokens are generated. And speculative decoding speeds up this generation -> speeds up RL.

summary:
Turing context into reusable skills for AI agents
THU, DeepLang AI and others introduced Ctx2Skill - a system that does this automatically and evolves skills in a self-improving loop.
Instead of read 200 pages again and again, the model can extract procedures, rules and strategies from them.
And here we encounter a multi-agent system once again.
Ctx2Skill creates a self-improving loop, where 3 agents play different roles:
1. Challenger: reads the context, creates hard questions/tasks, writes grading rubrics to expose weaknesses.
2. Reasoner: gets the context, uses the current skill set and attempts to solve the tasks.
3. Judge: compares the answer against the rubric and outputs simple feedback - pass or fail. No humans involved, no external labels needed.
Every failure becomes a learning signal: agents review what went wrong and convert it into new reasoning skills, expanding the model’s skill library over time.
In this setup the Challenger improves alongside the Reasoner, creating harder tasks.
And one more thing - there is no fine-tuning, because skills are inserted into prompts during inference and the system improves reasoning without changing model parameters.

title: Turing Post (@TheTuringPost)
summary:
Have you ever wondered what actually stands behind the idea of an AI workflow? Time to make it clear.
In organizations, the workflow is the unit you can actually inspect, automate, and improve.
And the most accurate definition would be this:
➡️ A workflow is a repeating sequence of decisions and actions that turns an input into an output, with points along the way where a human exercises judgment.
Judgement points matter! Strip those out and you have a pipeline – a cron job, a script, plumbing. Have them in and you have a workflow.
Most companies already run dozens of workflows across support, finance, engineering, sales, operations. But most of these workflows were never written down, many are informal and under-specified and exist because humans learned how to work around broken systems years ago.
LLMs change this. A lot of the gray area that previously required constant human coordination can now be handled through language, reasoning, classification, validation, and generation.
The interesting question becomes:
• Which judgment points can an agent handle?
• Which still require humans?
• How does the human know when to step in?
Across production systems we operate, the same patterns keep appearing: triage, monitoring, draft-and-review, execution-with-approval, investigation-and-recommendation, sync-and-transform, elicitation, curation
Interestingly, underneath all of them are the same primitives.
Together with @wschenk, we break down these primitives, recurring workflow patterns, and the full workflow taxonomy in this article →
Which workflow in your organization is already structured enough for an agent?

title: Turing Post (@TheTuringPost)
summary:
Embedded Language Flows (ELF) paper by @MIT researchers proposed a new approach to diffusion language models
The core idea is to keep generation continuous almost the entire time:
- ELF converts words into continuous embeddings
- Starts from random noise in that embedding space
- Gradually "cleans up" the noise into meaningful embeddings
- Converts embeddings back into words only at the very end
Other important decision used in ELF:
It's based on flow matching to allow the model learn a trajectory from random noise to clean language embeddings
Plus, the same network is used during denoising and for the final conversion of embeddings to tokens to make the system simpler and more efficient.
The advantages are also interesting
- better text quality
- fewer generation steps
- much less training data - 10× fewer tokens are needed compared to other models

title: Turing Post (@TheTuringPost)
summary:
Recently @pinecone introduced Nexus – a new knowledge-engine layer for AI agents that reduces token use by up to 90%.
It’s built on top of a vector database, but shifts reasoning earlier in the pipeline: from retrieval at query time to knowledge compilation before the agent even asks for information.
Instead of giving agents raw files, Nexus prepares task-optimized representations in advance.
These representations include artifacts – structured forms of information tailored to each agent’s specialization and workflow.
For example, a finance agent gets only billing schedules, pricing rules, and usage thresholds.
Pinecone’s VP of Product Jeff Zhu explains it like this:
"The artifact representation can range from markdown files to extracted entities to tables. These artifacts are then indexed for retrieval within Pinecone’s database which support both semantic, sparse, and full text search capabilities so that the right artifacts are retrieved during query time and then composed for the final structured output response from Nexus."
So vector databases are evolving from passive storage layers into active knowledge engines for agents.
Read this to learn what distinguishes vector database in the Agentic Era:

title: Turing Post (@TheTuringPost)
summary:
An interesting attention mechanism from @AIatMeta: SP-KV (Self-Pruned Key-Value Attention)
The model learns which tokens are likely to be useful for future attention and only keeps their key-value pairs in the persistent KV cache.
For every token and attention head, a small utility predictor (a 2-layer MLP) computes a utility score, and older tokens are selectively pruned based on it.
At the same time, attention becomes hybrid, because SP-KV still keeps a local sliding window fully available for short-range interactions
This approach:
- reduces KV cache size by about 3× to 10×
- allows to compress longer contexts more
- improves decoding speed and memory bandwidth

title: Turing Post (@TheTuringPost)
summary:
A new paper from @ylecun, @NadavTimor and others: "On Training in Imagination"
The main question of this study is: Given imperfect world models, imperfect reward models, noisy labels, and limited budget, how should we train most efficiently?
The researchers analyze two sources of error independently:
- Dynamics error → the imagined future is wrong.
- Reward error → the scoring of actions is wrong.
Here are the key findings:
• Models should have low Lipschitz constants → small input changes should produce small output changes, so smoother dynamics models, reward models, and policies lead to tighter error bounds and more stable imagined rollouts.
• With a limited training budget, the optimal allocation depends on which source of error decreases faster: more dynamics data vs more reward labels.
• Reward models scale much faster with data than dynamics models, likely because predicting a scalar reward is easier than predicting an entire future state
• In some cases, many cheap noisy reward labels are better than expensive accurate ones.
• But biased rewards are dangerous, because the policy gradient itself becomes biased, and you can't fix it.
So, in model-based RL, the structure and smoothness of the learned latent world matters as much as raw model accuracy.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HIkHXYCaUAAjdxv.png

title: Turing Post (@TheTuringPost)
summary:
Standard Transformers have fixed reasoning depth: information only flows upward through layers, so every token gets a limited number of computation steps.
TurboConn is a modified Transformer architecture that doesn't stop computation at each token.
→ It passes hidden states from deeper layers of token t back into earlier layers of token t+1.
This is cross-token recurrence rather than same-token feedback.
There are a lot of advantages in this approach:
- Reasoning depth grows with context length
- Later tokens can continue computations started earlier
- The reasoning stays fully latent (no additional CoT)
- TurboConn especially helps with tasks that depend on sequential state accumulation
- Accuracy improves by up to more than 10%
- On the Parity task a fine-tuned Qwen3-1.7B jumps from 53.78% to 100% accuracy
- All of this is achieved without retraining and complex curriculum learning
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HIoV3iubsAAQEmi.png

title: Turing Post (@TheTuringPost)
summary:
Attention in AI is a dynamic relevance computation in vector space.
Here’s what Transformers do step-by-step:
1. Tokens become embeddings that represent meaning. The Transformer starts with embeddings + positional encodings injecting word order information.
2. These vectors are projected into 3 representations:
Query (Q): what the token is looking for
Key (K): what the token exposes about itself
Value (V): the information the token can contribute
3. The model compares queries against all keys, searching for relevant tokens.
Higher similarity = higher attention
4. Then the model computes a weighted sum of the value vectors, producing a richer contextual representation for each token.
This process repeats across all layers and all tokens, gradually refining contextual representations.

title: Turing Post (@TheTuringPost)
summary:
Is Nathan the last one standing?
Quoting @natolambert
For a long time, academic researchers being at the cutting edge of new technologies has been a great social equilibrium. Neutral, unbiased technologists have been the people to spread new ideas to the world.
As AI research takes off in velocity, it is also going behind closed doors. The tech industry has sewed distrust, and now they are the ones trying to tell the world about incredible changes coming. It's a big loss to a form of social contract in America.
There's been a history of scientists helping society understand new technologies. There is a public service in the culture of science that I want to see continue.
It's being exacerbated by feelings of FOMO, especially finically driven, where I'm seeing many people who previously wanted to be professors -- and likely still do deep down -- feel a need to conform and chase money, in a pocket of industry. I get it, I grapple with this.
For those with a safety net, there will be great returns to some who choose to zag, and try to build something good, for people who need something different. For me, this is building interesting, fully-open models, to show what you can do with a variety of open weight sizes.
Yes, AI's immediate future is dictated by the frontier, but it's long-term trajectory still deeply includes academic institutions and open science. Knowledge will always diffuse, but to whom?
As of today, I think China is positioned to be the global home of AI research in a few years. The home of research is where ideas are accessible, spread rapdily, and are nurtured. The U.S. seems to be unwinding many institutions and relationships.
The largest returns go to people who build something differentiated, at least in reputation, and a lot of people are not being shown that this path exists.

title: Turing Post (@TheTuringPost)
summary:
Generative Recursive reAsoning Models (GRAM) – a reasoning model that goes both deeper and wider
This framework, introduced by @KAIST_AI, @Mila_Quebec and others, creates multiple possible reasoning paths in parallel, exploring different hypotheses and solution strategies at the same time.
Here are the main innovations:
• GRAM uses recursive latent reasoning instead of token-by-token chain-of-thought generation
• Repeatedly refines an internal latent state through recursive computation
• Adds controlled randomness (“stochasticity”) into the latent reasoning process.
• GRAM also adds probabilistic "guidance noise" to avoid getting stuck in a single trajectory.
This model separates reasoning into high-level abstract planning and low-level detailed computation.
Experiments show that this type of architecture improves performance on important tasks like Sudoku (97.0% accuracy), ARC-AGI, N-Queens (up to 99.7% accuracy), and graph coloring.

title: Turing Post (@TheTuringPost)
summary:
5 patterns for building long-running AI Agents
1. Checkpoint-and-Resume
→ Save progress in batches (like every 50 documents) so the agent can recover from failures without restarting entire workflows
2. Delegated approval
→ Long-running agents can “freeze” mid-process, preserve full context, and resume instantly once a human responds – even 24 hours later
3. Memory-layered context
→ Agents need separate working and long-term memory plus strict governance (identities, registries, access policies) to avoid memory drift and data leakage
4. Ambient processing
→ Don’t hardcode policies into agents – let background agents react to events in real time while pulling rules from a centralized governance layer
5. Fleet orchestration
5. Fleet orchestration for AI agents
→ Use a coordinator to orchestrate specialist agents, allowing components to run, scale and evolve independently. This prevents failures in one agent from cascading to others

summary:
Why KV cache is one of the main reasons LLMs are fast?
KV cache is what connects attention mechanism with generation stage of autoregressive models.
These models generate text token by token, but each new token still attends to all previous ones.
→ To optimize decode phase, models store previously computed key and value vectors in a KV cache.
→ During generation, they only compute new Q/K/V states for the latest token and attend over cached past representations.
Without KV cache, the model would recompute keys and values for the entire sequence at every step (like token 501 recomputes tokens 1–500), that's very slow.
▪️ But the tradeoff of KV cache is memory, because it grows with sequence length, batch size, layers, and attention heads.
That’s why so much research today targets KV efficiency and memory optimization. For example:
- Upgrading attention mechanism, since it influences how KV cache is formed. Use more advanced attention like CompactAttention, MHA, MLA, etc. based on your needs.
- Improve memory management. System needs to identify what to store long-term or keep local, when to summarize, and when to trim.

title: Turing Post (@TheTuringPost)
summary:
An interesting method for multi-reward RL
DVAO trains an LLM with several rewards at once, automatically deciding which rewards deserve more attention at each moment of training.
Everything depends on the strength of the learning signal ↓
For example, if you train a model for tool use, you care about: answer correctness, tool-call formatting, low hallucination rate, concise responses.
But these rewards are not equally useful at every moment of training.
So DVAO measures the variance inside the rollout group for every reward:
- high variance → the reward is informative
- low variance → the reward is currently less useful
Then it dynamically changes the weights: informative rewards get amplified, while weak or noisy rewards get suppressed. The model does it without manually tuning coefficients.
→ Importantly, DVAO does not treat rewards as fully isolated objectives. The update from a single reward is influenced partly by the model’s overall multi-objective performance on that rollout.
In practice, this prevents the model from over-optimizing one easy objective ignoring the others.
And the result is the best balance between accuracy and format/length compliance
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HJSZuspakAEQyig.png

clean_summary: KV cache connects the attention mechanism with the generation stage of autoregressive models. These models generate text token by token, with each new token attending to all previous ones. To optimize decoding, models store previously computed key and value vectors in a KV cache, so during generation they only compute new query, key, and value states for the latest token and attend over cached past representations. Without KV cache, the model would need to recompute keys and values for the entire sequence at every step, which is very slow. The tradeoff is that KV cache consumes memory, growing with sequence length, batch size, layers, and attention heads. This is why current research focuses on improving KV efficiency and memory management, such as upgrading attention mechanisms with variants like CompactAttention, MHA, or MLA, and developing better memory management strategies to decide what to store long-term, when to summarize, and when to trim. clean_title: Five patterns for building long-running AI agents
summary:
5 patterns for building long-running AI Agents
1. Checkpoint-and-Resume
→ Save progress in batches (like every 50 documents) so the agent can recover from failures without restarting entire workflows
2. Delegated approval
→ Long-running agents can “freeze” mid-process, preserve full context, and resume instantly once a human responds – even 24 hours later
3. Memory-layered context
→ Agents need separate working and long-term memory plus strict governance (identities, registries, access policies) to avoid memory drift and data leakage
4. Ambient processing
→ Don’t hardcode policies into agents – let background agents react to events in real time while pulling rules from a centralized governance layer
5. Fleet orchestration
5. Fleet orchestration for AI agents
→ Use a coordinator to orchestrate specialist agents, allowing components to run, scale and evolve independently. This prevents failures in one agent from cascading to others
Here's a full practical guide, including A2A and MCP interoperability →
by @addyosmani (Director at @GoogleCloud) and @Saboo_Shubham_ (Senior AI Product Manager at @google)

When Does LeJEPA Learn a World Model?
It's a new paper from @ylecun together with @klindt_david and @randall_balestr, that brings LeJEPA theory closer to the real goal of JEPA-style models.
→ LeJEPA learns a World Model when
• The world’s latent variables are Gaussian
• They evolve through stationary additive-noise transitions (and isotropic enough)
Under these conditions, LeJEPA can linearly recover the true latent variables from nonlinear observations.
So even if the data we see is a scrambled nonlinear version of reality, LeJEPA can learn a representation that undoes the scramble up to a rotation.

title: Turing Post (@TheTuringPost)
summary:
2. LeJEPA should learn h(z) = Qz
z is the true latent state and Q is an orthogonal rotation or reflection.
So the model does not need to recover the exact original coordinate system, but it must recover the same underlying structure.

title: Turing Post (@TheTuringPost)
summary:
3. Why this matters
If the representation is only a nonlinear scramble, then linear probes, planning algorithms, and downstream controllers may fail.
But if the representation is linearly identifiable, then:
- linear probes can recover the true latent variables
- latent-space planning becomes meaningful
- the learned state behaves like the real state
- control in representation space transfers to control in the true world
This is a feature of representation that is actually world-model-like.

title: Turing Post (@TheTuringPost)
summary:
4. LeJEPA's role
LeJEPA combines 2 objectives:
- Alignment loss: pulls positive pairs together
- SIGReg: pushes embeddings toward an isotropic Gaussian distribution
The model is trained to make related views similar, while keeping the embedding space Gaussian and non-collapsed.
And the paper shows this pattern → if the world has Gaussian latent variables, LeJEPA is forced to recover them linearly.

title: Turing Post (@TheTuringPost)
summary:
5. Why Gaussian latents?
Gaussian latents are the unique latent distribution where LeJEPA gets this linear identifiability guarantee under the paper’s assumptions.
For Gaussian worlds, the transition between positive pairs has a clean structure, including Gaussian noise and the variable that controls how correlated the two views are.
This is basically an Ornstein–Uhlenbeck transition.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HJcik7KaoAAf4Bo.jpg

title: Turing Post (@TheTuringPost)
summary:
6. Why does LeJEPA recover the latents?
It comes from spectral analysis. For Gaussian variables, any function can be decomposed into Hermite polynomial components:
- linear parts
- quadratic parts
- cubic parts
- higher-order
The paper shows that LeJEPA’s alignment loss penalizes every nonlinear degree more strongly, so the best solution is the linear one.

summary:
A search framework for stronger LLM reasoning – Bidirectional Evolutionary Search, or BES by @Harvard and @MIT
It combines:
- forward search to create and improve candidate solutions
- backward search to breaks the task into checkable sub-goals
+ BES can recombine parts of different candidate trajectories using evolution-style operators → Combinationб Deletionб Translocationб Crossover.
This helps to explore solutions that ordinary rollouts are unlikely to reach.
Due to backward the system can recognize partial progress even before the final answer is correct.
The most notable results:
- on MuSiQue multi-hop reasoning, BES improved Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct from 4.0% to 7.0% accuracy (GRPO degraded performance and Tree-GRPO barely helped)
- BES outperformed open-source evolutionary frameworks – OpenEvolve, GEPA, and ShinkaEvolve – on circle packing and Heilbronn convex optimization.

title: Turing Post (@TheTuringPost)
summary:
Agent harness performance doesn't scale reliably with raw test-time compute like tokens, tool calls, wall time, or cost.
Researchers from @HIT_1920 found that the key scaling variable is Effective Feedback Compute (EFC) – feedback that is informative, valid, non-redundant, and retained for later decisions.
Since tasks differ in how much feedback they require, the strongest predictor is usually EFC normalized by task demand.
• Harnesses improve when raw budget efficiently converts into durable, useful feedback through better routing, verification, memory, and observation quality.
• For real traces, repeated or unstable feedback must be discounted via NRS-EFC - non-redundant stable EFC.
Harness quality decomposes into 2 things: efficiency and sufficiency. So a good harness must both:
- Convert raw budget into useful feedback efficiently, measured by η = EFC/Craw (raw compute cost)
- Accumulate enough feedback relative to task difficulty, measured by EFC / Dtask (task demand)
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HJnA_Q3bwAALwV3.png

Breaking news: Cosmos 3 is here. They are attempting to do something completely new 🤯
Why is Physical AI much harder than building a chatbot?
Understanding the world is not enough, robots need to predict it and act inside it.
That's the idea behind NVIDIA Cosmos 3:
→ Reasoning model understands what's happening from video, images, text, and actions.
→ World model generates future states of the environment.
→ Action model generates the actions needed to achieve a goal.
Previous systems often stitched these capabilities together using separate models.
Cosmos 3 combines them into a single architecture with two components:
▪️ Reasoner Tower
Analyzes observations and builds an understanding of objects, motion, interactions, and physical context.
▪️ Generator Tower
Uses that understanding to generate future videos and action sequences that obey physical constraints.
So Cosmos 3 moves from:
Perception → Model A
Prediction → Model B
Actions → Model C
to:
Perception + Prediction + Actions → One unified system.
The goal is to make robots, autonomous vehicles, and smart environments better at answering three questions:
1. What is happening?
2. What will happen next?
3. What should I do?
That's a big shift from today's AI, which mostly focuses on generating text.
And check the benchmarks!
Physical AI needs to generate decisions that survive contact with the real world. 🚗🤖

title: Turing Post (@TheTuringPost)
summary:
Agent harness performance doesn't scale reliably with raw test-time compute like tokens, tool calls, wall time, or cost.
Researchers from @HIT_1920 found that the key scaling variable is Effective Feedback Compute (EFC) – feedback that is informative, valid, non-redundant, and retained for later decisions.
Since tasks differ in how much feedback they require, the strongest predictor is usually EFC normalized by task demand.
• Harnesses improve when raw budget efficiently converts into durable, useful feedback through better routing, verification, memory, and observation quality.
• For real traces, repeated or unstable feedback must be discounted via NRS-EFC - non-redundant stable EFC.
Harness quality decomposes into 2 things: efficiency and sufficiency. So a good harness must both:
- Convert raw budget into useful feedback efficiently, measured by η = EFC/Craw (raw compute cost)
- Accumulate enough feedback relative to task difficulty, measured by EFC / Dtask (task demand)

title: Turing Post (@TheTuringPost)
summary:
Breaking news: Cosmos 3 is here. They are attempting to do something completely new 🤯
Why is Physical AI much harder than building a chatbot?
Understanding the world is not enough, robots need to predict it and act inside it.
That's the idea behind NVIDIA Cosmos 3:
→ Reasoning model understands what's happening from video, images, text, and actions.
→ World model generates future states of the environment.
→ Action model generates the actions needed to achieve a goal.
Previous systems often stitched these capabilities together using separate models.
Cosmos 3 combines them into a single architecture with two components:
▪️ Reasoner Tower
Analyzes observations and builds an understanding of objects, motion, interactions, and physical context.
▪️ Generator Tower
Uses that understanding to generate future videos and action sequences that obey physical constraints.
So Cosmos 3 moves from:
Perception → Model A
Prediction → Model B
Actions → Model C
to:
Perception + Prediction + Actions → One unified system.
The goal is to make robots, autonomous vehicles, and smart environments better at answering three questions:
1. What is happening?
2. What will happen next?
3. What should I do?
That's a big shift from today's AI, which mostly focuses on generating text.
And check the benchmarks!
Physical AI needs to generate decisions that survive contact with the real world. 🚗🤖

summary:
.@perplexity_ai made search code-driven and agent-controlled with a new architecture - Search as Code (SaC).
The agent stops being stuck with one big monolithic search API, and generates Python code that composes search primitives for the task.
SaC architecture includes 3 main layers:
• Model as control plane
Decides the search strategy, decomposes the task and generates code.
• Secure compute sandbox
Generated code runs here and it's where it can batch, filter, dedupe, retry, aggregate, and manage intermediate state.
• Agentic Search SDK
The SDK exposes search primitives: retrieval, ranking, filtering, fanout, parsing, rendering, and access to intermediate search signals.
▪️ New features that come with SaC:
- Programmable search pipelines: retrieval, ranking, filtering, fanout, dedupe, parsing, and aggregation can be combined dynamically.
- Task-specific retrieval: the agent adapts the search strategy per problem.
- Massive parallel search: workflows can trigger hundreds or thousands of retrieval operations efficiently.
- Intermediate noisy results can be processed in code before reaching the model for lower context pollution.
So, SaC is a perfect addition to the agentic search methods from here:

clean_summary:
@TheTuringPost reports that @perplexity_ai has developed a new architecture called Search as Code (SaC), which makes search code-driven and agent-controlled. Instead of relying on a single monolithic search API, the agent generates Python code to compose search primitives tailored to the task.

SaC consists of three main layers: a model as control plane that decides the search strategy and generates code; a secure compute sandbox where the code runs and manages intermediate results; and an agentic Search SDK that exposes primitives like retrieval, ranking, filtering, and aggregation. New features include programmable search pipelines, task-specific retrieval, massive parallel search, and processing of noisy intermediate results before reaching the model. This architecture enhances flexibility and efficiency in search-driven AI agents, complementing existing agentic search methods.

summary:
Super interesting announcement: Project Solara. #MSBuild
Microsoft’s thesis is that if agents become the primary way we interact with software, they should not be confined to laptops and smartphones.
Project Solara is a platform for building agent-first devices.
The company showed two early concepts:
• a desktop AI companion that sits on your desk and provides direct access to your agents
• a wearable badge with cameras, microphones, sensors, and secure authentication that can observe, document, retrieve information, and trigger actions on your behalf
What caught my attention is that Microsoft is explicitly avoiding the question of “the next device.”
Instead, it argues that there won’t be a single successor to the smartphone.
Different industries have different workflows. A nurse, a retail employee, a lawyer, and a field technician do not need the same hardware.
What they may need is access to the same agent infrastructure.
In many ways, Solara feels like Microsoft’s answer to a question raised by Humane, Rabbit, Meta glasses, and a growing list of AI hardware projects.

title: Turing Post (@TheTuringPost)
summary:
2 tools for scientific figure generation and editing – Crafter and CraftEditor↓
They wrap image gen in a better agentic workflow:
1. Crafter – a multi-agent harness for scientific figures
> makes targeted corrections
> keeps structured memory of the figure
> works with paper/context, reference images, sketches or instructions
> outputs a raster figure + a structured figure specification
> supports text-to-image, sketch refinement, mask completion, and key-element composition
> uses 5 cooperating agents: intent reasoner, plan generator, critic, specification refiner, convergence judge
2. CraftEditor – a raster-to-SVG conversion system
> Turns flat figures into editable SVGs
> This enables local edits to labels, colors and layout without regenerating the whole figure
CraftEditor first breaks a raster image into meaningful parts, then uses grounding to detect where each component is and reconstructs the layout as layered SVG elements.

.@perplexity_ai made search code-driven and agent-controlled with a new architecture - Search as Code (SaC).
The agent stops being stuck with one big monolithic search API, and generates Python code that composes search primitives for the task.
SaC architecture includes 3 main layers:
• Model as control plane
Decides the search strategy, decomposes the task and generates code.
• Secure compute sandbox
Generated code runs here and it's where it can batch, filter, dedupe, retry, aggregate, and manage intermediate state.

- Task-specific retrieval: the agent adapts the search strategy per problem.
- Massive parallel search: workflows can trigger hundreds or thousands of retrieval operations efficiently.
- Intermediate noisy results can be processed in code before reaching the model for lower context pollution.
So, SaC is a perfect addition to the agentic search methods from here:

summary:
Peter’s broader vision goes far beyond @openclaw itself.
I met with Omar @OmarShahine today and he explained to me, what it is:
“OpenClaw is only one piece of a larger ecosystem he is building around AI-native software development.
The core idea is that letting AI write code is not enough. If software is going to be generated by agents, the surrounding systems become critical: testing, verification, security, reliability, and maintainability. The challenge shifts from writing code to proving that the code is safe and correct.
A lot of Peter’s work focuses on building those guardrails. He has created systems for automated testing, security scanning, validation, and change verification, so that AI-generated modifications can be evaluated before they reach production. The goal is to create a development environment where agents can move quickly without sacrificing quality.
*What makes it particularly interesting is that he treats software development itself as a greenfield problem.* Rather than adding AI to existing workflows, he is exploring what software engineering looks like when agents are involved in every stage of the process. New tools, new workflows, and new engineering practices are emerging almost weekly.
It feels like the industry is collectively discovering a new way to build software, and the pace of learning is extraordinary.”
Thank you, Omar, for an interesting conversation!
(Omar has a dream job, by the way. He leads development of the Scout Agent at Microsoft, built on OpenClaw, and is also an OpenClaw maintainer 💪🏼)

title: Turing Post (@TheTuringPost)
summary:
Who is the better reviewer – AI or a human?
45 scientists spent 469 hours judging 2,960 individual review criticisms from humans and AI across Nature-family papers and found that:
→ AI reviewers surfaced 26% of issues humans missed
→ GPT-5.2 beat the top human reviewer
BUT
> AI reviewers agreed with each other far more than humans did and shared recurring blind spots
> The strongest human advantage is correctness.
Top human = 92.3% correctness, while AI reviewers were lower: GPT-5.2 – 86.2%, Claude Opus 4.5 – 83.7%, Gemini 3.0 Pro – 81.9%.
> Humans still win on field norms and long context
So the most important advantage of AI is diligence: checking code, statistics, evidence, and hidden inconsistencies humans often don’t have time to inspect.
But anyway it's not replacing humans, AI's the reviewer humans didn’t know they needed.

title: Turing Post (@TheTuringPost)
summary:
Vector Policy Optimization (VPO) – a new policy optimization method that optimizes for a diverse set of good answers
Each one is good at different parts of the reward signal.
Here is how it works:
1. For a prompt and an answer, instead of using one reward score, VPO assumes a vector reward.
2. Each component measures one aspect of answer quality, e.g. different test cases, criteria, reasoning steps, or user preferences.
3. The model produces multiple candidate answers for the same prompt
4. VPO checks different ways of weighting the reward components, so different answers can be useful under different trade-offs
5. The model is rewarded when its set contains answers that are strong under different reward weightings.
6. This encourages the model to produce a collection of answers that work well together as a search pool.
Another good feature is that VPO can be also used inside GRPO → GRPO updates the model, but VPO decides what reward GRPO should optimize.
VPO scores the whole answer set by checking which answers are best under different reward weightings, then uses that score for the GRPO update

title: Turing Post (@TheTuringPost)
summary:
Who is the better reviewer – AI or a human?
45 scientists spent 469 hours judging 2,960 individual review criticisms from humans and AI across Nature-family papers and found that:
→ AI reviewers surfaced 26% of issues humans missed
→ GPT-5.2 beat the top human reviewer
BUT
> AI reviewers agreed with each other far more than humans did and shared recurring blind spots
> The strongest human advantage is correctness.
Top human = 92.3% correctness, while AI reviewers were lower: GPT-5.2 – 86.2%, Claude Opus 4.5 – 83.7%, Gemini 3.0 Pro – 81.9%.
> Humans still win on field norms and long context
So the most important advantage of AI is diligence: checking code, statistics, evidence, and hidden inconsistencies humans often don’t have time to inspect.
But anyway it's not replacing humans, AI's the reviewer humans didn’t know they needed.

GitHub was built for developers collaborating with developers. But now it needs to be reimagined human-agent collaboration – from UI to UX to AX (agent experience).
Our @Kseniase_ has talked to @mariorod1, Chief Product Officer at @github, who has the most clear vision of the changes.
He explains the inflection point that hit around December 2025: models finally got good enough that developers could micro-delegate to agents without always correcting them.
And that’s why he says:
"GitHub’s mission is advancing human progress through developer collaboration. And now we probably need to say developer and agent collaboration."
We also discussed:
• how GitHub is dealing with explosive agent traffic and 3x growth patterns
• why the future developer may simply be a builder with intent
• the new Copilot app and “canvases” where humans and agents co-create in real time
• why parallelization is overrated
• and why Copilot will stay copilot, not pilot, with the human in the loop
Mario’s version of the future is more open – he sees agent-native coding as giving more people access to creation.

OpenProse – an open-source "logical English" language that turns your agentic workflows into reusable agent programs.
It runs inside the coding agent you already use: Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Hermes, Pi – and gives it a structured contract to follow.
→ The key idea – the coding agent becomes the "compiler".
This delivers:
- Less babysitting of multi-agent coding sessions
- Reviewable .prose.md programs instead of disposable prompts
- Explicit skill and tool dependencies
- Isolated sub-agent sessions with clean outputs
- Run receipts, logs, artifacts, and audit trails
- Reuse of sessions on demand
So OpenProse extracts the entire workflow: phases, contracts, decision gates, loops, parallel work, mistakes, fixes, and validation evidence. It's like a “git for agent workflows”.

title: Turing Post (@TheTuringPost)
summary:
AutoScientists – a research lab made of agents
@Harvard researchers connected agents into a self-organizing scientific team without a boss agent standing in the middle
All agents look at the same shared workspace: they share memory, explore multiple directions in parallel, critique each other, avoid repeated failures, and reorganize as evidence changes.
But the teams are not fixed. Agents can gather around a promising direction, like architecture, optimizer changes, or data augmentation, then abandon it if it stops working.
Before they spend compute, they discuss proposals and critique each other.
AutoScientists also shows strong results:
- 74.4% mean leaderboard percentile on BioML-Bench
- 1.9× faster GPT training optimization
- +12.5% on ACE2–Spike, with the same method transferring to 217 ProteinGym assays for a +6.5% average gain

.@axiommathai has pushed formal verification beyond pure math into economics.

▪️ The project starts with a formalization of Robert Aumann’s famous "agreeing to disagree" theorem.
But AxiomProver didn't just verify the proof. It uncovered a hidden assumption: requiring every information cell to have positive probability makes Bayesian updates possible, and it also quietly forces the information structure to be countable.
In other words, the system was doing "assumption accounting," exposing exactly which assumptions make the result work.
▪️ The team also formalized the Monderer–Samet p-belief extension, where disagreement becomes possible but quantitatively bounded.

A true research highlight
Researchers from @Harvard, @MIT and others built an LLM agent "economy"
Their system is called Economy of Minds and it replaces orchestration with economic incentives. Agents:
→ bid in auctions for the right to act
→ pay each other
→ gain virtual wealth from rewards and spend it
→ mutate if successful
→ and go bankrupt if ineffective
▪️ And surprisingly, coordination emerges automatically.
Agents specialize, cooperate, and develop multi-step reasoning strategies without being explicitly told how to work together.
Why?
The idea comes from Friedrich Hayek → Markets coordinate knowledge without central planning.
Now we're seeing the same principle applied to AI. That's why we need to start building better economies instead of smarter manager agents.
There’s another proof that this path is effective – the large performance gains of Economy of Minds:
• Math reasoning: 15.9% → 57.0%
• Financial research: 45.0% → 60.0%
• Scientific research: 5.0% → 20.0%
• Accelerator design: 2× better energy-delay tradeoff
• Distributed systems: 657 vs 930 optimization cost

title: Turing Post (@TheTuringPost)
summary:
Wow, this is interesting..
@Stanford researchers put a common assumption to the test: large models need only “high-quality” filtered training data.
What if the best filter is no filter at all?
They compared full Common Crawl data with heavily filtered versions of it and got surprising results:
1. Filtering can help with small compute budgets, because models can't learn from everything well.
2. However, as models get larger and train longer, the full, unfiltered dataset becomes the winner.
Large models handle messy data better than expected – low-quality text, irrelevant text, or some “junk” data are not a big deal; these models can tolerate them.
And they can even extract useful signal from data that looks poor.
These facts transform general rules:
→ Filtering helps when compute is limited. But when compute is very large, removing too much data may throw away useful information.
This also connects with the concept of "bitter lesson": at large scale, simple scaling often beats clever human design.
But the final choice depends on your constraints and preferences – would you rather increase compute costs or put more resources and time into filtering?
Interesting to see your answers 👀
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HKknB30bAAA6XII.jpg

summary:
.@GoogleDeepMind just released a 57-page report on a question that not many people discuss now:
What happens after AGI?
→ ASI (artificial superintelligence) systems more capable than large groups of human experts
DeepMind sees 4 possible paths from AGI to ASI:
• Scaling compute, models, and data
• New AI architectures, paradigms and methods
• Recursive self-improvement (AI improving future AI)
• Collective superintelligence – multi-agent coordination, where many AGI-level agents work together and form ASI.
These paths aren't mutually exclusive and could happen at the same time.
But ASI would still have limits and wouldn't be all-knowing. Possible issues are:
- Energy, hardware, physics and infrastructure constraints
- "Data wall"
- Too expensive scaling
- Current neural-network approaches can hit a ceiling
- AI research is becoming harder itself
- AI may struggle to discover fundamentally new concepts beyond human knowledge (the "abstraction barrier")
- Regulation, governance, and societal pushback
Predicting ASI progress is highly uncertain now, especially while we're still far from AGI.
But the paper is a strong call to action: we need better forecasting, better benchmarks, and more research into post-AGI development.
And the future is likely to look more like a series of accelerating breakthroughs across science, technology, and research.
This research is definitely worth reading if you're interested in long-term AI trajectories

summary:
An open-source Agent Reinforcement Trainer (ART) – plugs GRPO into any Python app
→ Your app defines the task and reward
→ ART handles the RL loop: inference, trajectory scoring, GRPO optimization, checkpointing and LoRA updates
So agents learn through experience and environment interaction.
It's useful for multi-step tasks like tool use, email search, MCP, games and reasoning workflows
For example, ART•E trained a Qwen 2.5 14B email agent that outperformed OpenAI's o3 on email retrieval
▪️ The core loop looks like this:

title: Turing Post (@TheTuringPost)
summary:
What powers AI on iPhones, Macs and @Apple's cloud?
Now it's AFM 3 - Apple's new generation of 5 AI models with up to 20B-parameters.
→ The core idea: How did they make a huge advanced model work on a phone or laptop without requiring enormous memory?
There are 2 solutions:
1. Instruction-Following Pruning (IFP) :
- AFM 3 stores most of the model in flash storage (SSD/NAND) instead of adding RAM and large GPUs
- Keeps shared knowledge loaded
- Swaps in only the task-specific parts when needed.
This allows AFM 3 Core Advanced to activate only 1–4B out of 20B parameters.
2. Elastic size – the AFM 3 scales itself to the problem:
Simple request → activate fewer experts
Difficult request → activate more experts
So today AFM 3 family including 2 on-device and 3 cloud models sits behind Apple Intelligence, Siri, image gen, dictation, etc. thanks to these features.
Results of these models have also improved:
- AFM 3 Core Advanced upgrades text-to-speech quality from 3.87 to 4.15 MOS and wins dictation evaluations 44.7% to 17.6% over Apple's previous system.
- AFM 3 Cloud Pro shows +10% response satisfaction and +14% math performance over AFM 3 Cloud.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HLYQjzXagAAwyZg.jpg

clean_title: Concerns about Claude Tag's security, lock-in, and cost implications
summary:
That’s a very interesting take on Claude Tag.
The main concern: pervasive security risk and lock in with unclear token consumption
Quoting @random_walker
The new Claude Tag feature seems extremely useful, but at the same time, a dangerous bargain for enterprises because of the pricing model and the risk of lock-in. The four big changes together mean that you interact with Claude as a coworker instead of a tool (the same Claude instance for everyone instead of each worker; soaks up tacit knowledge without your telling it; acts on its own; and does so asynchronously). All clearly very useful, but completely flips the interaction paradigm.
Let’s talk about lock-in. As far as I can tell, Claude maintains its own memories in this new way of working; the human team members can’t see and edit them. (System administrators presumably can, but they have other things to do!) Tacit knowledge thus goes from a weakness of AI agents to a major strength — it seems inevitable that as teams and orgs start to use Claude this way, it will become the main queryable repository of all their tacit knowledge, creating dependence and stickiness. Effectively, Claude is a coworker that you can’t fire without *every* team losing workflows and know-how.
By the way, it also seems to introduce a new and pervasive security risk, since Claude can be integrated into private channels as well, and can be given access to repositories and tools even if the users in that channel don’t have access to them. Anthropic has introduced an interesting but complicated access control model to handle all this: But I’m not sure I trust people to understand and implement it correctly, nor the LLMs to be sufficiently robust against threats like prompt injection.
What about pricing? Claude is not like regular coworkers, because it bills for every token it produces. And it can do an unbounded amount of work, asynchronously and without being asked. In the current model, when AI is a tool, enterprises set per-user budgets, which creates accountability and keeps cost somewhat manageable. When everyone shares a Claude, it will be much harder to track and control spending. Of course you can set a token budget, but turning off Claude for the month for everybody when the budget is hit risks bringing work to a screeching halt.
When AI companies talk about the next stage of AI being a “drop-in replacement” for human workers, it should be understood not as a technical innovation but a business model innovation, enabling more value capture and rent extraction. AI companies are no longer competing for a share of enterprises’ IT budgets but rather a share of their entire labor spend, which is orders of magnitude bigger. Claude Tag is a big milestone in this evolution. This shift is very good for AI companies, but it is unclear if it is good for their customers.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HLlEOOkXsAAx2W1.png
clean_summary:
That’s a very interesting take on Claude Tag. The main concerns are the pervasive security risks and potential lock-in with unclear token consumption.

The new Claude Tag feature makes Claude behave more like a coworker than a tool, with shared memories and autonomous actions, which could lead to dependence and stickiness as tacit knowledge becomes a main repository of organizational knowledge. It also introduces security risks, as Claude can be integrated into private channels and granted access to repositories and tools without user awareness, raising concerns about access control and prompt injection threats.

Pricing is another issue: Claude bills for every token it produces and can perform unbounded work asynchronously, making it difficult to track and control costs. When AI shifts from a tool to a shared coworker, it reflects a business model change aimed at capturing more value from enterprise labor spend, which may benefit AI companies but could be problematic for customers.

title: Turing Post (@TheTuringPost)
summary:
"Quantized Reasoning Models Think They Need to Think Longer, but They Do Not"
@AIatMeta found a weird failure mode in quantized reasoning models:
▪️ They don’t just get cheaper and less capable – they start overthinking.
In up to 52% of failures, the model actually reaches the correct answer halfway through its reasoning... then talks itself out of it.
It spirals into hesitation with "wait," "but," "maybe," and new branches.
Why does this happen?
Quantization mainly affects high-uncertainty decoding steps.
It makes hesitation tokens much more likely to be sampled, sending the model into unnecessary self-reflection.
→ Meta proposed a very simple fix: apply a small decoding penalty to about 50 hesitation tokens. No retraining.
Results:
• 12–23% shorter Chain-of-Thoughts
• Up to 58% fewer overthinking errors
• Accuracy is often preserved (or even improved) across math, coding, and science benchmarks.
So knowing when to stop is almost as important as knowing how to reason.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HMRPE-ObQAAkuYC.png

title: Turing Post (@TheTuringPost)
summary:
One of the most practical MCP papers we've ever seen
It's useful for anyone building MCP servers who's unsure how to structure them well.
Here are the main tips:
1. Don't use too much tools, because tool-selection accuracy drops below 90% after 10–30 tools.
2. See MCP servers as a software architecture problem.
The researchers documented 5 emerging architecture patterns:
• Resource Gateway – exposes existing data sources through MCP
• Tool Orchestrator – coordinates multiple tools behind a simpler interface
• Stateful Session Server – maintains conversation or workflow state across requests
• Proxy Aggregator – combines capabilities from multiple MCP servers into one endpoint
• Domain-Specific Adapter – wraps a complex external API into LLM-friendly tools
It's also interesting that MCP itself adds almost no latency (0.01 ms via stdio, 0.39 ms via HTTP). So real-world performance is mostly limited by the network.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HManAhTbQAAri53.png

summary:
NVIDIA is betting that agentic AI's next bottleneck isn't the GPU – it's the CPU!
It just unveiled Vera – a new CPU architecture already being tested by AI companies such as Perplexity, alongside its next-generation Rosa CPU with the upcoming Rigel core.
▪️ Basically, CPUs execute the work around AI models.
While GPUs run neural networks, CPUs handle everything between model calls: tool use, code execution, data processing, KV-cache management, retrieval and result verification.
For AI agents, this work sits on the critical path.
• Every agent follows a loop: reason → execute a tool → analyze/verify → reason again.
• Each step depends on the previous one, so the speed of a single CPU core affects how quickly an agent completes its task.
More CPU cores increase throughput, but not single-agent speed.
➡️ Agentic AI benefits from maximum single-threaded performance.
NVIDIA’s Vera represents this new CPU class:
• 88 custom Olympus cores
• Up to 1.2 TB/s LPDDR5X memory bandwidth
• 3.4 TB/s core-to-core bandwidth
• 50% higher instructions per cycle than Grace
Results are:
• 1.8× higher sustained per-core performance than leading x86 CPUs on agentic workloads
• In Perplexity’s tests: 1.5× faster coding workflow and up to 1.9× faster concurrent sandbox startup
Now CPUs are evolving alongside GPUs and TPUs, because autonomous agents depend not only on how fast GPUs run models, but also on how fast CPUs execute each agent step.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HMqh2ZYbsAECjm4.jpg

title: Turing Post (@TheTuringPost)
summary:
Can AI agents reproduce the diversity and bias of human scientific analyses? 👀
Yes.
One of the most interesting AI-for-science papers, “The Agentic Garden of Forking Paths” from @Stanford, found that:
Different AI "researchers" assigned different personas reach different conclusions from the same dataset, reproducing much of the ideological variation seen among human research teams.
But this didn’t happen because of obvious methodological mistakes.
86% of the AI analyses passed independent AI review, and 78% were judged methodologically sound by human experts.
The bias appeared at 2 stages:
1. Agents explored different analytical paths
2 Then they selected results that matched their assigned beliefs
So the main issue is hidden uncertainty: the same data can support multiple reasonable analytical paths.
That's why the researchers also introduced the m-value.
-> It estimates how unusual a reported conclusion is within the space of all plausible analyses.
That's actually a way to understand where a published result sits among all the other reasonable analyses that also work
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HMzpBy6aoAAiHJb.png

There was a reason why I highlighted it, and I didn’t see it mentioned in other coverage.
I was testing Pets, and here is what I discovered. It was a quick but telling test:
Different Pets produced utterly different results. The idea, structure, language, what to address, and what to discuss were so different that it felt like using a different model.
The formatting was also completely different, but that is more explainable. One of them was Codex, so you can assume it would use a more programming-like structure.
Why do I think this is important?
There are ten Pets. Then there are six levels of effort and two speed options. That gives us up to 120 possible combinations.
This will either be super convenient, once you know what each Pet is good at and which settings work best for each task, or completely confusing, because first you need to test them all on a bunch of similar tasks.
Pets look like a fun customization feature. But they might actually change how we interact with the model, and make choosing the right interface a task of its own. #openai @sama

title: Turing Post (@TheTuringPost)
summary:
There was a reason why I highlighted it, and I didn’t see it mentioned in other coverage.
I was testing Pets, and here is what I discovered. It was a quick but telling test:
Different Pets produced utterly different results. The idea, structure, language, what to address, and what to discuss were so different that it felt like using a different model.
The formatting was also completely different, but that is more explainable. One of them was Codex, so you can assume it would use a more programming-like structure.
Why do I think this is important?
There are ten Pets. Then there are six levels of effort and two speed options. That gives us up to 120 possible combinations.
This will either be super convenient, once you know what each Pet is good at and which settings work best for each task, or completely confusing, because first you need to test them all on a bunch of similar tasks.
Pets look like a fun customization feature. But they might actually change how we interact with the model, and make choosing the right interface a task of its own. #openai @sama
Quoting @TheTuringPost
We've got access to ChatGPT 5.6. Who cool is that?!

title: Turing Post (@TheTuringPost)
summary:
Compete Then Collaborate
A very interesting paper on training small coding models.
The author have Claude, Gemini, Codex, and Grok first compete against each other, then collaborate to build a shared curriculum.
Models' answers are judged through actual code execution, not an LLM judge
▪️ The main findings are surprising:
- SFT on the teachers’ solutions does not improve the student and can even hurt performance.
- On competition problems, performance dropped from 5.9% to 2.9%.
- But when the same curriculum was used as an RL environment with verifiable rewards, performance increased to a peak of 8.8%.
That's why AI teachers' potential is worth exploring. They may evolve from generating training data to building verifiable environments where models learn by doing.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HNUCANkaQAA4Tsa.png
